name: extensible-visitor
intent: Keep the visitor open on both axes at once - new element kinds and new operations arrive without editing or recompiling any visitor that already exists - by giving every visitor a default method that catches element kinds it was not written for, introducing extended element kinds under an intermediate base whose accept hooks overload (not override) accept, and extending an operation by subclassing the existing concrete visitor so it inherits every case it already handled.
problem: A classic Visitor is cheap in one direction only: a new operation is a new visitor, but a new element kind forces every visitor to grow one more method, so shipped visitors must be edited and redeployed. The trigger is an element hierarchy that is extended by parties who do not own the operations - language dialects, plugin node types, versioned grammars, third-party message formats - where the existing operations must keep working unchanged on the extended structure.
context: Recursively defined element hierarchies (abstract syntax trees, intermediate representations, document and message models) that grow over time, in a statically typed language whose visitors are concrete classes or interfaces with default bodies, and where the traversal logic itself lives inside the operations. It pays off when old operations must run against new element kinds and when element kinds are added by a different team than the operations; it assumes the visitor protocol can carry a default case and that a runtime type test is acceptable on the dispatch path.
benefits: Both dimensions stay open: a new element kind is handled by extending the element hierarchy and, where needed, by extending an operation, while visitors written earlier keep compiling and running against the new structure.
Element kinds can be contributed by a different team than the operations - no central list of visitors has to be edited, so extensions ship independently and old binaries keep working.
Operation implementations are reused by inheritance rather than copied: an extended visitor inherits the complete existing behaviour and adds only the cases it cares about.
Old visitors degrade deliberately instead of failing: the default case lets tooling such as printers, validators and serializers keep working on element kinds that predate them.
The visitor protocol can be versioned explicitly, so a visitor can state which element kinds it was written against and the bridge can route both old and new clients.
Dispatch stays a double dispatch: elements still choose the operation method, so element code does not accumulate operation-specific branches.
tradeoffs: The default case converts a compile-time guarantee into a runtime one: a visitor that forgets a case silently falls through to the default instead of failing to compile, which is exactly the property the classic Visitor is valued for. Unless the default throws, correctness depends on tests and documentation.

Reaching the extended visitor requires a runtime type test - dynamic_cast, is/as?, Any::downcast_ref, an interface assertion - so the compiler no longer proves that a visitor can handle the element it is handed.

Extending an operation means subclassing a concrete visitor, which couples operations to each other's implementation: state, caching and recursion of the base visitor leak into every extension, and a change to the base can break its descendants.

Recursion must be virtualized: an operation that creates another visitor while traversing has to do so through an overridable factory method, otherwise the extension is lost below the first level - discipline a plain Visitor never needs.
Types multiply: every extension adds an intermediate element superclass, an extended visitor protocol and, in the versioned form, another bridge, so the class graph grows a layer per version.
Which visitor version handles which element kinds lives in documentation and tests rather than in the type system; the mapping is easy to get wrong when several extension branches exist.
Abbreviating the runtime test - casting straight to the extended element type - compiles and then fails on the first element from an unforeseen branch, so the savings are paid back at the worst time.

participants.responsibility: Base of the visited hierarchy; declares the accept hook that starts double dispatch and, in the default-based form, routes unknown kinds to the visitor's default method.
Implements accept by calling the visitor method that names its own type, the second half of the dispatch pair.

Intermediate type introduced by an extension; its accept hooks take the extended visitor protocol (overloading, not overriding accept) so new kinds reach the new methods while old visitors still see them as base elements.
The operation protocol: one method per element kind plus one default method that handles every kind the visitor was not written for.
Protocol that inherits the visitor's methods and adds one method per new element kind, keeping old implementers and new clients in one type relation.
One implementation of one operation over the element hierarchy.
Subclass of an existing concrete visitor; inherits its behaviour for the kinds it knows and overrides the default case to re-dispatch new kinds to the new methods.
Overridable method through which a visitor obtains further visitor instances during traversal, so an extension is preserved at every recursion depth.
Walks the structure and hands one visitor instance to the elements, choosing the version and implementation of the operation.

use_cases: A compiler front-end whose node kinds are extended by language dialects while every existing analysis pass keeps running unchanged (the extensible-compiler case the pattern was derived from).
An IDE or linter analysing a versioned language grammar: the version-1 analysis must not be recompiled when version 2 adds syntax nodes it does not understand.
Plugin systems where third-party modules contribute new node types (document formats, workflow elements, protocol messages) to a host that ships the operations.
Optimisation or lowering pipelines whose passes are shipped separately from the node hierarchy: the platform team adds representations, users add passes.
A published visitor API where other teams implement visitors and the element set grows every release, making 'which kinds does this visitor handle' an explicit, versioned contract.
Migration and validation tooling that must keep working on messages produced by newer producers than the tool itself.

Serialization and schema-generation frameworks such as Jackson's JsonFormatVisitor API, which uses a visitor to traverse Java type hierarchies for JSON/XML schema generation and allows third-party serializers to contribute handlers for new POJO shapes without modifying the core framework.

Query engines over tree-structured data (e.g. Apache Calcite's relational algebra, Rascal's AST analysis): new relational operators or AST node types are contributed by extension modules while existing optimisers and evaluators continue to function unchanged.

Static analysis and bug-finding tools (Coverity, CodeQL, ESLint plugin architectures): new checker plugins add new node-type coverage while the core traversal engine ships unchanged, and old checkers degrade gracefully over unknown node types.

Game engine entity-component systems: new component types are contributed at runtime while existing systems (physics, rendering, AI) continue to process entities; the visitor with default case handles component types added after a given system was written.

Python's ast.NodeVisitor: visit() dispatches to a visit_<Node> method and falls back to generic_visit as the built-in default case, so analysis tools written before newer node kinds existed (Match, TryStar, TypeAlias) keep traversing Python's evolving AST unchanged, exactly the degrade-don't-break contract of the pattern.

The JDK Compiler Tree API (com.sun.source.tree.TreeVisitor / SimpleTreeVisitor): every visit method defaults to visitOther/defaultAction as the catch-all, so javac-based tooling written against Java 8 trees keeps compiling and running as Java adds records, patterns and switch labels - old visitors land in visitOther instead of failing.

Roslyn's CSharpSyntaxVisitor / CSharpSyntaxWalker: the generated visitor carries one Visit method per syntax node kind plus DefaultVisit as the default case, and each C# language version extends the node hierarchy while existing analysers and the compiler's own passes keep working over the extended tree.
avoid_when: The element set is closed and the language can check it: a sealed hierarchy plus exhaustive matching proves coverage at compile time and retires the visitor (Kotlin, Scala and Swift enums, Java 17 sealed types, Rust enums, TypeScript discriminated unions).
Only new operations are ever needed: a plain Visitor, or plain polymorphic methods on the elements, gives the same benefit with no casts and no default-case risk.

Runtime type information is unavailable or forbidden (RTTI disabled, hard real time, a codebase rule against casts): use the plain Visitor while the element set is stable, or the acyclic visitor when visitors must stay independent of elements.
The data type is owned by one team and changes rarely while operations change daily: folds or plain functions over a closed type are smaller than a dispatch protocol.
There are one or two operations over a shallow structure: direct methods or a dispatch table are simpler than double dispatch with a default case.
The extension mechanism would be used to avoid designing the hierarchy at all: an element set that grows weekly usually wants a closed model plus data-driven handling, not more visitors.
anti_patterns: Silent default: implementing the default case as an empty body, so every unforeseen element kind is skipped without a trace and the operation reports success on data it never examined.

Cast and hope: extending the default case with an unchecked downcast to the extended element type; the code is correct until an element from another extension branch arrives, then it throws or corrupts state.
Hard-coded construction: an operation that instantiates its own concrete visitor while recursing, which makes every subclass silently lose its extension one level down.

Default everywhere: pushing nearly all cases into the default handler to avoid writing visit methods, which throws away the visitor's only compile-time benefit and leaves a type switch with extra steps.
Version inflation: adding a visitor interface per change without a factory or bridge discipline, so clients must guess which version to implement and the published API surface doubles per release.
Extensible visitor as a substitute for a stable model: using subclass hooks to keep an element hierarchy permanently half-designed instead of closing it once the shape is known.
design_principles: Open/closed principle in both directions: extend the element hierarchy and the toolkit without modifying what already exists.
Single responsibility: operations live outside the element classes, and each extension adds only the cases it needs.
Dependency inversion: elements depend on the visitor protocol rather than on concrete operations, and an extension depends only on the previous version of the protocol.
Liskov substitutability: an extended element must still satisfy the base element's contract for visitors that predate it - that is precisely what the default case is for.
Interface segregation across versions: a visitor written against version N sees exactly the element kinds of version N.
Protected variation: the extension points (default case, visitor factory) are isolated so the rest of the protocol can stay stable.
best_practices: Make the default case explicit and loud: throw, or record a diagnostic, unless a genuine no-op is correct for every element kind that may appear later.
Virtualize every recursion: an operation that needs another visitor instance during traversal must get it from an overridable factory, never from a hard-coded constructor.
Keep each visitor version's reach honest — implement every new case or route it deliberately to the previous default — and document which kinds the version knows.
Keep the runtime type test in exactly one place, the element's dispatch path or the extended default case, and never scatter casts through operation code.
Test both cross-version paths explicitly: an old visitor applied to new elements (default path) and an extended visitor applied to old elements (inherited path).
Prefer a new pure visitor protocol per version over adding default members to a shipped one, unless the language's default members are the only way to avoid breaking existing implementers.
Close the hierarchy instead of versioning it when the toolchain can prove coverage; keep the extensible visitor for hierarchies that genuinely stay open.

Think of a visitor as a fold with accumulation: the element hierarchy defines the recursion shape, the visitor defines what is accumulated at each node and how the partial results combine — this perspective makes it easy to see when an operation is a visitor versus when a simpler traversal suffices.

Apply the 'tell, don't ask' principle: a visitor should tell an element what to compute, not query the element's internal state; if your visitor is doing instanceof or getter chains, the operation likely belongs inside the element as a dedicated method.

In performance-sensitive traversal (hot compiler passes, real-time game loops), avoid allocating visitor instances per node — reuse a single visitor with mutable accumulation state, or use an iterative stack instead of recursion to prevent call-stack overflow on deep trees.
sources: Krishnamurti, Felleisen & Friedman, 'Synthesizing Object-Oriented and Functional Design to Promote Re-Use', ECOOP 1998 — the Extensible Visitor pattern: extend elements and tools without modifying existing code, by subclassing visitors and giving them a default case.
Zenger & Odersky, 'Extensible Algebraic Datatypes with Defaults', ICFP 2001 — the encoding of extensible visitors with default cases, overloaded accept and factory methods for virtualized recursion.

Zenger & Odersky, 'Independently Extensible Solutions to the Expression Problem', EPFL technical report 200433 / FOOL 2005 — the Scala encoding, plus the critique that cast-based extension is unsafe and that defaults must exist on both sides.

Wadler, 'Expression Problem', 1998 (email) / OOPSLA 1998 talk — the foundational statement of the problem that extensible visitor solves: independently extending data variants and operations without recompiling existing code.
Gamma, Helm, Johnson & Vlissides, Design Patterns (1994) — Visitor: the stable-element-set assumption this variation deliberately relaxes.

Conway & Chow, 'The Extensible Visitor Pattern in Tagless Final Style', 2019 — a Haskell encoding showing how extensible visitors map to type-class-based denotational semantics, separating the signature of operations from their implementation.
Eli Bendersky, 'The Expression Problem and its Solutions', 2016 — practical TypeScript/Python walkthrough of visitor, extensible visitor, and sealed-hierarchy approaches with performance benchmarks.
Apidesign Wiki, 'Case Study of Writing the Extensible Visitor Pattern' — practitioner account of applying the pattern in a real API design, with Java implementation.

Robert C. Martin (Uncle Bob), 'Acyclic Visitor' — the original article introducing the acyclic visitor variant to break the element-visitor dependency cycle at the cost of dynamic_cast and without default-case elegance.
Nice Language Wiki, 'Visitor Pattern Considered Useless' — critique of visitor as workaround for missing multimethods, with comparison to multi-methods as a cleaner alternative.
pitfalls: Silent default: implementing the default case as an empty body, so every unforeseen element kind is skipped without a trace and the operation reports success on data it never examined.

Cast and hope: extending the default case with an unchecked downcast to the extended element type; the code is correct until an element from another extension branch arrives, then it throws or corrupts state.
Hard-coded construction: an operation that instantiates its own concrete visitor while recursing, which makes every subclass's extension silently lose its extension one level down.

Default everywhere: pushing nearly all cases into the default handler to avoid writing visit methods, which throws away the visitor's only compile-time benefit and leaves a type switch with extra steps.
Version inflation: adding a visitor interface per change without a factory or bridge discipline, so clients must guess which version to implement and the published API surface doubles per release.
Extensible visitor as a substitute for a stable model: using subclass hooks to keep an element hierarchy permanently half-designed instead of closing it once the shape is known.

Hierarchy pollution: applying extensible visitor to a hierarchy that is actually stable and closed, adding default-case machinery and versioned protocols that will never be needed, inflating the codebase with complexity that only pays off when the element set genuinely grows.

Shy Visitor: mixing the visitor with instanceof or type checks inside visit methods, undermining the double-dispatch mechanism and making the code brittle to new element kinds — if an element type check appears inside a visitor, the visitor is not fully doing its job.

Cyclic dependency creep: as versions accumulate, each new element base and visitor protocol creates an additional compile-time dependency; without disciplined layering (element base → extended base → ...; visitor protocol → extended protocol → ...) the graph becomes a tangle that resists static analysis and slows incremental compilation.

Wrong move: trusting a generated visitor's default case (Roslyn DefaultVisit, TreeVisitor visitOther, ast generic_visit) to be safe for every tool -> the default silently returns null or keeps walking, so an analysis reports clean on language syntax it never examined -> instead treat the default path as a version contract: log, flag, or raise when the kinds crossing it are not on the list the operation claims to cover.

Wrong move: shipping one visitor interface forever and bolting new cases on with default methods -> implementers can no longer tell which element-kind version they target, and old binaries break with missing-method errors the moment a non-default abstract method appears -> instead publish a new pure interface per version plus an internal bridge that routes old and new clients.

Wrong move: making every future kind land in an inherited superclass so the base hierarchy never has to be finished -> the default case becomes the design, dispatch degenerates into a scattered type test, and each extension branch adds a dependency edge no one can audit -> instead close the hierarchy (sealed types, exhaustive match) as soon as the shape is known and reserve extensibility for kinds a real external contributor adds.
